item.title: China-Russia energy ties highlighted
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-05
China-Russia energy ties highlighted Xi, Putin encourage more collaboration in congratulatory messages to forum President Xi Jinping has expressed China's readiness to deepen energy cooperation with Russia and make joint efforts to keep the industrial and supply chains in the energy sector stable and unimpeded. He made the remarks on Friday in a congratulatory letter sent to the 8th China-Russia Energy Business Forum, which was held in Vladivostok, Russia. In the message, Xi noted that this year marks the 30th anniversary of the establishment of the China-Russia strategic partnership of coordination and the 25th anniversary of the signing of the China-Russia Treaty of Good-Neighborliness and Friendly Cooperation. He said that amid a complex and evolving international landscape, the China-Russia comprehensive strategic partnership of coordination for a new era has maintained high-level development. The fruitful energy collaboration has promoted the common development of both countries, becoming a model of mutually beneficial cooperation, he added. Emphasizing that the global energy landscape is undergoing profound adjustments, with opportunities and challenges intertwined, Xi said that China stands ready to work with Russia to continuously deepen energy cooperation and jointly safeguard the stability of industrial and supply chains in the sector. Russian President Vladimir Putin also sent a congratulatory message to the forum, highlighting that energy has traditionally been one of the most important and dynamic areas of economic cooperation between Russia and China. Russia firmly holds the top position among suppliers of oil and natural gas to China and is also a leading exporter of coal and liquefied natural gas to the country, according to a statement published on the official website of the president of Russia. "The construction of several Russian-designed nuclear power units in China is nearing successful completion. Joint technological innovations are also being developed to improve the efficiency and environmental safety of hydrocarbon production, processing and trans-portation," Putin said. He expressed hope that the forum will be substantive and productive, and that the ideas and initiatives the participants put forward will be translated into practical actions. Amid continued volatility in global energy markets, China and Russia are accelerating the structural deepening of their energy partnership, anchored by stable fossil-fuel supply chains, while simultaneously breaking ground in next-generation clean-energy corridors. Pipeline cooperation remains central to their cooperative relationship. Also, one of the most closely watched developments came in April this year, when Chinese and Russian companies signed cooperation agreements related to a proposed cross-border hydrogen freight corridor. On Friday, Vice-Premier Ding Xuexiang and Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak co-chaired the 23rd meeting of the China-Russia Energy Cooperation Committee in Vladivostok. Ding highlighted the steady growth of energy trade between the two countries, saying that major landmark cooperation projects have progressed smoothly and new advancements have been made in clean energy cooperation. Ding emphasized the importance of jointly advancing the transformation of the global energy governance system and making greater contributions to energy security and sustainable development for both countries and the world. Novak highlighted the important role of strategic guidance of the two heads of state in the growth of bilateral trade and in maintaining the stability of the energy supply chain. He said that Russia is willing to work with China to optimize existing cooperation projects, expand and plan new areas of cooperation for the next phase, and make new contributions to deepening pragmatic cooperation. caodesheng@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: China eyes top spot again at 20th Asian Games
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-05
China eyes top spot again at 20th Asian Games China's 815-strong team of athletes, led by a blend of Olympic champions and rising young talent, is gearing up for the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026, aiming to finish atop both the gold medal and overall medal tables for the 12th consecutive time. With 27 percent of its athletes born in 2005 or later, the young Chinese delegation will compete at the continental multisport event in Japan from Sept 19 to Oct 4, using the Games as an important test on the road to the 2028 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles. The 1,274-member delegation — which includes competitors, coaches and support staff — was officially announced in Beijing on Friday. Gao Zhidan, head of the delegation (chef de mission) and minister of the General Administration of Sport of China, called on team members to compete with determination and strive for excellence in their athletic performance and sportsmanship. "We will stay focused on our goals, lift our spirits, fight tenaciously and strive for the best possible results," Gao said. Team China consists of 404 women and 411 men, with an average age of 24. They will compete in 38 sports and 369 medal events. The youngest athlete is 12-year-old skateboarder Cao Shiqi, while 41-year-old shooter Wan Antao is the oldest. Fifty-eight athletes from 17 ethnic groups are also included. A total of 548 athletes will make their Asian Games debuts. Meanwhile, 306 members of the squad have competed in previous Olympic Games, Asian Games or both. Thirty-six Olympic champions from 13 sports are among the competitors. Table tennis stars Sun Yingsha and Wang Manyu, divers Chen Yuxi and Wang Zongyuan, gymnast Zou Jingyuan, canoeist Sun Mengya and weightlifter Li Wenwen are among the established champions expected to lead China's medal challenge while helping guide younger teammates. Seventeen-year-old sprinter Chen Yujie represents the delegation's emerging generation. In August, she set an Asian U20 record of 11.08 seconds in the women's 100 meters at the 2026 Chinese Athletics Championships, and she will compete in both individual and relay events at her first Asian Games. "Stepping onto the Asian Games stage for the first time, I want to compete fearlessly and perform at my best," Chen said, adding that she hopes competing against Asia's top athletes would help her gain experience for the 2028 Summer Olympics. Passing on experience to a new generation is also a key theme within the delegation. For diving Olympic champion Wang Zongyuan, his second Asian Games will serve as a "midterm examination" ahead of the Los Angeles Olympics. "I hope to pass on our techniques, spirit and strength of character to more young athletes," Wang said. Olympic weightlifting champion Shi Zhiyong, who is now a coach, will also draw on his experience at major competitions to help younger athletes perform at their best levels. Zhang Xin, secretary-general of the delegation, said that China remains the frontrunner in Asian sporting competitions, with Japan and South Korea close behind, while countries including India and Kazakhstan have also made rapid progress in several events. Although China's delegation this time around is smaller than the one sent to the 19th Asian Games Hangzhou, held in Zhejiang province in 2023, Zhang said the team remains confident of achieving its goals. The delegation will also compete in four sports not to be included in the 2028 Los Angeles Olympic program — wushu, breaking, karate and esports — hoping to promote traditional Chinese culture through wushu and showcase the diversity of the country's sporting development. As a key test in the Los Angeles Olympic cycle, the Aichi-Nagoya Games will provide China with a valuable opportunity to assess its preparations, gain experience at a major multisport event and demonstrate the potential of its next generation of athletes. liyingxue@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Medical personnel testing soil to prevent epidemics
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-05
Medical personnel testing soil to prevent epidemics Medical and epidemic prevention personnel from the Chinese military have begun testing soil samples from the core area of the mudslide-hit Gyirong Port in Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region, to help formulate disinfection and personal protection plans as detailed search and rescue efforts continue. Bacterial culture and pathogen testing are being used to gauge the risk of infectious diseases for rescue crews working amid shattered rocks and thick sludge in the core area, said a medical and disease prevention team with the People's Liberation Army Xizang Military Command's logistics support department. The road access was largely restored on Wednesday morning. Lhamo Tsering, a military technician specializing in infectious disease prevention and control, said that soil samples collected from the core zone would go through testing for 21 vector-borne pathogens, 23 respiratory pathogens and 32 gastrointestinal pathogens. "Conducting pathogen testing on these soil samples can identify the types and levels of soil pathogen contamination, assess the risk of secondary infectious diseases, trace the sources of pollution, and guide environmental disinfection and personnel protection," she said. "The results can also help us evaluate the effectiveness of epidemic control efforts and prevent the spread of soil-borne infectious diseases after a disaster," she added. Liu Xiaonan, a member of the team, was among the first to enter the core zone on Wednesday after the road leading to the port reopened. He recalled heavy downpours that evening, and his team worked until late before returning. One of the most challenging parts of his work was navigating the deep mud in the area. "In some areas, the sludge looks solid, but when I try walking on it, my feet can get sucked down until the mud comes up to my calves or even my knees. Sometimes we are only able to pull ourselves out with the help of nearby personnel," he said. It is also important to prevent mosquito and other insect bites in the area, he added. Lhamo Tsering was one of the two female military personnel working on-site on Friday morning. The other was tasked with providing psychological consulting for search and rescue crew members. Lhamo Tsering said she had participated in responding to acute health emergencies, including the COVID-19 outbreak, in the past. It was her first time working on the front line in the aftermath of a devastating natural disaster of this scale. "I am used to performing tests in the laboratory using samples collected and transported back by my fellow soldiers. This time, I asked to come to the hardest-hit area because I wanted to collect the samples myself to ensure the precision of my work," she said. As a native of Lhasa, the regional capital of Xizang, Lhamo Tsering said she was also deeply saddened by the havoc wreaked by the mudslide at Gyirong Port. "This area is naturally beautiful with pristine air, a comfortable altitude and lush vegetation," she said. "I hope that one day it can restore its beauty." item.title: Media's future tense in AI-driven world
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-05
Media's future tense in AI-driven world An apartment door arrogantly demands a payment before it opens or closes — and threatens a lawsuit when an angry visitor tries to unscrew it. The scene from Philip K. Dick's science-fiction novel Ubik may have appeared fantastical when the book was published in 1969. But nearly six decades later, artificial intelligence-powered machines have brought the idea closer to reality. And if Elon Musk is right, AI would deliver "abundance" to the world. For the media, that period of plenty has already arrived — with devastating effects. Across the world, traditional media organizations are struggling as algorithms, platforms and AI reshape how information is produced, distributed and consumed. The paradox is striking: while the abundance of information is creating enormous wealth for big tech companies, even enabling them to challenge sovereign powers, human society is besieged by information of uncertain credibility. The central question for traditional media is not whether AI will change the industry. It already has. The question is what role professional media can play in a world where information is abundant, but truth, context and reality are increasingly scarce. Dick sounded a useful warning. During his lifetime, he was not recognized by the mainstream science fiction community, suffered from constant depression and died in penury. Yet, his writing anticipated a future of unstable realities and the dystopia of dehumanization with extraordinary prescience. Another of his works, The Man in the High Castle, is particularly relevant here. It imagines an alternate world with a different version of reality. Today, the dominance of personalized algorithms, social media, misinformation, propaganda and AI-generated content shows that an alternate reality itself can be created. Traditional media was built over centuries around institutions, professional standards and regulations designed to establish facts and uphold the truth. It has been swept aside by algorithmic personalization and AI-generated content. Dick's novels raise the specter of a darker possibility of the AI age. His characters don't merely disagree on politics or other issues. They even disagree about what reality is. The real danger is not that machines will produce false information, but that people will become increasingly comfortable living inside alternate realities constructed for them. And they will defend this version of reality even if the truth may be quite different. Dick's vision also has an important lesson: human beings adapt. It is here that The Man in the High Castle unexpectedly connects with the ancient Chinese I Ching, or Book of Changes. The two are separated by centuries and cultures, but both point to a profound idea: reality is not necessarily fixed; it is a pattern of constantly changing possibilities. The I Ching, whose origins date back more than two millennia, is an ancient Chinese system of making decisions during uncertainty. The question is not, "What will happen?" Instead, it is, "What kind of situation am I in, and how should I respond to its changing pattern?" That could be the role the media needs to play in the age of AI. If there is abundant information, it loses its scarcity and, with it, much of its economic value. What remains scarce is the ability to determine what matters, what is credible and what it means. Not all science fiction is about dystopian futures. From Isaac Asimov to Gene Roddenberry, many writers have also imagined technology helping humanity overcome its limitations. Asimov famously proposed three laws of robotics, attempting to establish principles that would keep machines from harming humans. The first law said a robot may not injure a human or let a human come to harm through inaction. The second law stressed that robots must obey humans, provided they don't violate the first law. The third law laid down that robots must protect themselves, unless doing so broke the first two laws. These laws reflected the belief that human beings could impose rules on technologies. But we now know that the race for AI supremacy is far more complicated than the threats from robots Asimov imagined in 1942. Roddenberry's Star Trek offered an even more ambitious vision: a universal civilization that has overcome scarcity, conflict and even the pursuit of wealth. In Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home, Captain Kirk and Spock travel back in time to 20th-century San Francisco in search of a humpback whale whose survival is essential to saving Earth in the 23rd century. At one point, marine biologist Gillian Taylor asks Kirk whether people in his time still used money. "Well, we don't," replies the captain. The world is far from being moneyless as yet. But AI-driven abundance is increasingly making it a possibility. Remember how Google turned the world upside down with the free-of-charge model for search and maps? AI's moneyless world may just be round the corner. So, what will be the role of money in the world? It will continue to be used for natural resources, especially minerals, if the prophecies of science fiction works such as Alien, Red Mars, Avatar and Total Recall prove true. These visions of the world offer hints for traditional media to navigate the future. In a dystopian future as described in Dick's novels, the media could become an I Ching for humanity, helping people navigate uncertainties, distinguish reality from illusion and make informed choices when there is no single agreed version of the truth. If the future is enlightened as envisioned by Roddenberry, the media could help humanity understand how to live with abundance created by AI in a universal civilization. The challenge for traditional media is how it can finance itself in the first scenario, and inspire itself in the second. In The Man in the High Castle, Dick warns that humanity's "destiny lies in the hands of a few men". We can only hope that some of them are traditional media editors. The author is an advisor to the Pacific Economic Cooperation Council for Thailand and an editor of Asia News Network. The views don't necessarily represent those of China Daily. Shenzhen: Soaring to new heights as a 'sky city' Share - WeChat
Shenzhen is rapidly evolving into a "sky city", where the low-altitude economy is seamlessly integrated into everyday life. Drones swiftly deliver packages, efficiently perform traffic patrols, and transport medical supplies across the city. At the heart of this transformation is Bao'an district, an innovation hub that is generating new jobs and fueling economic growth. With its drones making a global impact, Shenzhen is embracing openness and innovation, marking just the beginning of its journey as a "sky city".

item.title: Relief efforts intensified in disaster area
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-05
President Xi Jinping urges all-out rescue, relief efforts after mudslide hits border port in Xizang Level-II emergency response activated after mudslide hits border port in Xizang Until last month, Hao Zhen had only seen disaster relief efforts on the news. Then a devastating mudslide struck Gyirong, the remote border county in Xizang autonomous region where he works as a volunteer. The 27-year-old was among 17 volunteers from China's Go West program who joined relief efforts in Gyirong township after the Aug 26 disaster. While professional rescue teams searched the hardest-hit areas, Hao and his fellow volunteers worked behind the scenes, arranging accommodation, distributing supplies and helping provide meals for displaced residents and rescue workers. "When the disaster first happened, a lot of affected residents and rescuers arrived in the township all at once," Hao said. "The first thing we had to do was make sure they had somewhere to stay and food to eat." As relief supplies poured in, the volunteers counted, sorted and moved thousands of boxes donated by Red Cross organizations, companies and foundations. They also helped with logistical work at the local emergency response headquarters and collected and organized information from the disaster area. The experience gave Hao a new understanding of what disaster relief involves. "Before this, I had only read news stories about volunteers helping after disasters," he said. "Now I realize that you don't have to be on the search-and-rescue front line to make a difference. Keeping things running behind the scenes matters, too." Born in 1999, Hao is the oldest of the 17 Go West program volunteers working in Gyirong township. Most of the others were born between 2000 and 2003. They come from across China, including Heilongjiang, Jiangxi and Shandong provinces, as well as Xizang, and have backgrounds ranging from medicine to education. The work has come with practical challenges. Only two of the 17 volunteers speak Tibetan, creating communication difficulties at the shelters. Local township officials often stepped in to interpret. Food and accommodation were also stretched in the first few days as large numbers of residents, rescuers and support workers arrived in the small border town. Hao said the situation gradually improved as local authorities coordinated with hotels and restaurants to provide additional support. Another five Go West program volunteers remained in the county seat, helping receive relatives of missing people, assisting families and handling calls and follow-ups through the 12345 public service hotline. Volunteers from nearby counties, including Lhaze and Dingri, also came to help. For Hao, Gyirong is a long way from home — nearly 5,700 kilometers from Shuangyashan in Heilongjiang province. He usually makes the journey home only once a year. He arrived in Gyirong in February 2025 to join the Go West program and plans to stay for three years. His family initially tried to talk him out of the move, worried about the distance and the physical demands of living at high altitude. "But I thought, if everyone worries about the hardship and the distance, places like this will have fewer and fewer young people willing to come," Hao said. The physical challenges are real. When Hao first arrived in Gyirong, he found he did not have the same stamina he had at lower elevations. He also experienced heart palpitations when he first joined the relief effort. After more than a year on the plateau, however, he said his body has largely adapted. His family still worries about him, particularly after learning that he was involved in the disaster response. "But the disaster happened right here, where we work and live," Hao said. "Since we chose to come here as volunteers, helping when something like this happens is simply part of what we should do." The Aug 26 mudslide at Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border was triggered by an ice-rock avalanche originating from a high-altitude glacier in Nepal. As of Friday evening, 31 people had been confirmed dead and 531 remained missing in Gyirong, according to the local emergency response and rescue command headquarters. For Hao, the experience has also changed the way he sees the small tasks that fill much of his day. Moving boxes, arranging accommodation and making sure people have meals may be far removed from the dramatic scenes of a search-and-rescue operation, but he no longer sees them as minor jobs. "My biggest hope now is that we can keep the support work running smoothly, that all the rescuers return safely and that there are no more secondary disasters," he said. KATHMANDU -- Nepali rescuers on Saturday rescued a Chinese national from a hydropower plant hit by the deadly mudslide in Nepal, according to the Chinese Embassy in Nepal. The Chinese national was rescued by the Nepali Army in coordination with a disaster expert team from South Korea, 11 days after a devastating mudslide struck the area. The survivor was taken for further medical assessment and care. The rescue is part of an intensified effort to locate and evacuate people believed to be trapped inside hydropower project tunnels following a mudslide that swept through the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river systems. The disaster caused extensive damage to several hydropower projects and other infrastructure in the affected areas. Some workers and other people are believed to have been trapped inside hydropower tunnels and have remained out of contact. Before the rescue of the Chinese national, the Nepali Army said in a social media post that a joint rescue team comprising 20 Nepali Army personnel and project representatives had been conducting search operations. The Nepali Army has been conducting search and rescue operations in coordination with foreign technical teams, including experts from China, India and South Korea, to reach people stranded inside structures at several hydropower projects. China has deployed around 20 sets of monitoring equipment across the disaster-hit Gyirong area in the Xizang autonomous region, with real-time data showing geological conditions stabilizing, a senior geologist said. The devices — including debris flow monitors, slope radars and microseismic sensors — were installed by the China Geological Survey and other emergency response teams following last month's ice-rock avalanche that buried parts of the Gyirong border crossing, causing massive casualties on both sides of the border. Ge Daqing, deputy director of the China Aero Geophysical Survey and Remote Sensing Center for Natural Resources, said the equipment was positioned at key risk points across the disaster zone to monitor slope movement, debris flow channels and ground deformation in real time. Two additional slope radars were installed on Wednesday near the border crossing after rescue teams cleared access roads, he added. The devices are positioned to protect workers repairing roads and power lines by issuing early warnings if falling rocks or shallow landslides are detected on the slopes above. Data collected so far indicates the dynamic processes at the site have entered a relatively stable phase. "Overall, there have been no significant fluctuations or changes," Ge said, adding that the risk of a large-scale secondary disaster is currently assessed as low without external triggers. However, he cautioned that high-risk factors persist due to the complex terrain. Some minor rockfalls have been observed at the glacier front in the collapse zone, but Ge said these pose no immediate threat. The monitoring equipment is primarily intended for the emergency response phase. Once a comprehensive risk assessment is completed and no major threats remain, the devices may be withdrawn, he said. Beyond the immediate response, the disaster has underscored the limitations of existing monitoring technologies in the high-altitude, cloud-prone Himalayan region. Ge said optical satellite imagery — the most common remote sensing tool — is severely hampered by persistent cloud cover and fog in the area. Clear images can be obtained on only about 20 days a year, and most of the optical data received recently have been obscured by clouds. To address this, Ge called for the accelerated development of new synthetic aperture radar satellites, particularly an interferometric SAR satellite constellation that combines L-band, high-resolution, wide-swath capabilities, and both sun-synchronous and low-inclination orbits. This can overcome the challenge of monitoring rapid deformation in the high-elevation mountains and glaciers of the Himalayas. He also stressed the need to improve satellite revisit cycles and spatial resolution to enable more frequent and rapid monitoring. Unmanned aerial vehicles offer another monitoring option, but current drones struggle to operate above 7,000 meters and their sensors remain vulnerable to cloud interference. New radar-based sensors and improved high-altitude flight capabilities are needed, he added. Looking ahead, Ge warned that the risk of high-altitude ice-rock avalanches in the region is likely to increase. "The 2015 Nepal earthquake caused internal damage to these mountain masses," he said. "Combined with glacial erosion at high elevations and steep terrain, the structural integrity of rock formations has been compromised, making them prone to collapse." Given the transboundary nature of such hazards, Ge highlighted the importance of international collaboration in disaster monitoring and early warning across the Himalayan region, noting that ice-rock avalanches and glacial lake outburst floods do not respect national borders. limenghan@chinadaily.com.cn The death toll from the massive mudslide that struck a border port in Gyirong county, Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region, on Aug 26, rose to 31 as of 6 pm on Friday, while 531 people remained missing. A total of 987 personal items had also been recovered, according to the disaster emergency and rescue command headquarters. The rescue access route to Gyirong Port has been opened, marking a new stage in relief efforts, the headquarters said at a news conference on Friday evening. The command center said coordinated rescue operations would be further intensified, with particular emphasis on monitoring and early warning for secondary disasters at the port site and along the G216 highway. Local authorities will also continue to assess risks and issue early warnings for areas upstream and downstream of the disaster site to ensure the safety of rescue operations, the headquarters said. Since the mudslide hit Gyirong Port, an important land gateway between China and Nepal, round-the-clock rescue operations involving multiple government departments have been underway. As of 4 pm on Wednesday, 172 experts and technicians from meteorological, natural resources, water resources and emergency management departments, along with 150 sets of equipment, had been deployed to the site, according to the headquarters. The water resources authority, for example, sent 28 experts with 31 sets of equipment, including drones, radar water-level gauges and high-definition cameras, to conduct hydrological monitoring. The natural resources department dispatched 92 technicians with 40 sets of equipment to carry out focused surveys along two rescue access routes and in areas affected by the mudslide. The regional government has also moved swiftly to assess geological hazards in the disaster area. As of Wednesday, a special inspection along the G216 highway, a key rescue access route, had identified 58 geological hazard sites. Seven were classified as high-risk, 39 as medium-risk and 12 as low-risk, according to the headquarters. Local authorities have completed hazard inspections and risk assessments in three affected villages and identified two sites for temporary shelters, while providing guidance on their construction, the headquarters said. Technology has played a key role in the rescue operation. Slope radar, high-definition video surveillance and geophone monitoring systems have been installed in areas affected by ice-avalanche debris flows to continuously detect anomalies, including ice-rock collapses and deformation of debris in the source zone. By automatically collecting deformation and image data, the systems help address the limitations of manual inspections in the steep, canyon-locked terrain. They enable real-time monitoring of key hazard sites and help ensure the safety of rescue personnel working downstream, the command center said. In addition, local authorities have established a regular coordination mechanism to ensure smooth information flow throughout the rescue operation. Despite his weary appearance, he insisted repeatedly that he was not tired at all. "All I want is to find my workmates," he said on Thursday, gripping an iron shovel with determination, his brow furrowed. On Aug 26, a massive mudslide devastated Gyirong Port, a vital land link between China and Nepal. By Wednesday noon, 21 victims had been found, 847 personal belongings recovered, and 541 people remained missing. Xiao was driving toward the port when the disaster struck. "I was just four or five kilometers away when I saw several cars pulled over," he said. "I got out and asked other drivers what was happening — everyone was panicked, saying the water level had risen sharply near the port." Concerned for their safety, he instructed the two female colleagues in his car to get out and find a safe place, then continued driving alone to assess the situation. Upon realizing it was a landslide, Xiao immediately alerted the authorities. "The muddy water was rushing toward me, so I threw the car into reverse and backed up about 500 meters before stopping," he recounted, his voice tense. "I was terrified the car would be swept away. What really scared me was not knowing what had happened to my workmates at the port." As visibility dropped sharply and the road ahead was blocked, Xiao found himself trapped. Reflecting on that moment, he said, "I really walked through the gates of hell that day." Driven by worry and a deep sense of duty, Xiao joined the rescue teams. By Sunday, he had reached the vicinity of the port and immediately immersed himself in the relief efforts. "As soon as I arrived, I started moving supplies, then began searching. I found clothing, shoes and crushed vehicles belonging to the missing. Every single item I saw pierced my heart like a needle." Originally from Qinghai province, the 39-year-old Xiao has worked in Xizang for 17 years, with 11 of those years at the Gyirong entry-exit border inspection station, primarily handling publicity affairs. "For many years, I've spent almost every day with my workmates — filming their patrols, writing about their lives guarding this border," he said. "This port, these people — they've become part of me." On the first day of the rescue, Xiao and other workers camped in a tent by a reservoir halfway up the mountain near the border port. He did not sleep at all. "The rain was so heavy that night — water poured down the slopes and merged into the river. The sound of rain, rushing water, and collapsing hillsides all mixed together. It made my heart sink. I didn't dare to sleep, and I couldn't sleep anyway," he said. As he spoke, he picked up the shovel and resumed digging. Unmanned aerial vehicles offer another monitoring option, but, currently, drones struggle to operate above 7,000 meters and their sensors remain vulnerable to cloud interference. New radar-based sensors and improved high-altitude flight capabilities are needed, he added. "The 2015 Nepal earthquake, which exceeded magnitude 8, caused internal damage to these mountain masses," he said. "Combined with glacial erosion at high elevations and steep terrain, the structural integrity of rock formations has been compromised, making them prone to collapse." "Every major disaster should teach us something beyond the emergency response itself," Ge said. "We need to build resilient disaster prevention systems — in urban planning, engineering design and settlement siting — that account for a wider range of geological hazards." The Chinese People's Liberation Army and the People's Armed Police Force have deployed hundreds of personnel and specialized equipment to assist emergency search and rescue operations following the catastrophic mudslide in Gyirong county, Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region. The mudslide, which occurred on Aug 26, has caused significant casualties and left many people missing in the region. In response, military forces immediately activated emergency response mechanisms to support local authorities in disaster relief efforts, Jiang Bin, a spokesman for the Ministry of National Defense, said at an online news briefing on Friday. As of Thursday, a total of 726 service members, 24 pieces of construction machinery and 60 specialized equipment sets had been mobilized to the affected areas in Gyirong. Over 20 helicopter and drone sorties have been executed to facilitate operations, according to Jiang. "Rescue personnel have focused their efforts on searching for survivors, reopening blocked roads, delivering critical supplies and providing emergency medical care," Jiang said. Over 13,900 cubic meters of mud and rock had been cleared. Additionally, 77 relief personnel and 1.23 tons of essential supplies had been airlifted directly into the disaster-stricken core area. The military has also provided healthcare and disease prevention services to local residents and rescue workers on more than 900 occasions. "Putting the people and human life above all else, our military forces remain on the front lines of rescue efforts, racing against time to locate missing individuals and minimize casualties," Jiang said. "So long as there remains a single glimmer of hope, we will never give up." Zhangmu Port in Nyalam of Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region, will adjust its customs and border inspection facilities from Saturday to improve safety management for the high-altitude mountain environment, according to an announcement by the local government on Thursday. Located in a deep Himalayan valley, the port is a major land gateway between China and Nepal. Its mountainous terrain exposes the area to geological hazards. The adjustment is aimed at protecting inbound and outbound travelers and their property, while maintaining normal border clearance operations and orderly movement through the port. Starting at 10 am on Saturday, customs and immigration inspection operations at Zhangmu Port will be moved to the port's former temporary inspection area for import cargo. The road section connecting the Friendship Bridge border gate to the new inspection site will be designated as a controlled port area and a customs transit supervision zone, with closed-loop management implemented. Under the new arrangement, cross-border travelers will be transferred through designated routes. They will not be allowed to leave the designated area, move around freely, get on and off vehicles midway, or have unauthorized contact with people outside the designated transfer system. Without permission, vehicles will not be allowed to stop along the controlled section to pick up or drop off passengers or load or unload goods. Unrelated personnel and vehicles will also be barred from entering the area. Authorities said that the change only concerns the layout of customs and border inspection facilities. The port's opening status and bilateral customs clearance policies will remain unchanged. Following the glacier-collapse mudslide that struck Gyirong Port in Xizang autonomous region, China's meteorological authorities swiftly deployed portable ground-based weather observation facilities near the port, providing real-time weather support for rescue efforts. Fire and rescue teams are expanding detailed searches across the core disaster area around Gyirong Port in Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region, after the main land route was reopened, allowing heavy machinery to support deeper excavation and searches, the Ministry of Emergency Management said on Thursday. National Highway G216 was fully reopened to the core area on Wednesday morning. Rescue personnel, supplies and heavy equipment have since moved in, shifting operations from largely manual surface searches to deeper and more targeted searches. The State Grid announced that after power crews worked around the clock, temporary power lines to the core area of Gyirong Port were fully restored on Thursday evening, ensuring electricity supplies for rescue and relief operations in the area. The mudslide struck Gyirong Port on Aug 26 after originating on the Nepalese side of the China-Nepal border. As of noon on Wednesday, 21 victims had been found and 541 people remained missing. The disaster also knocked local base stations out of service, severed sections of main power lines and cut roads, electricity and communications to the hardest-hit area. After days of repairs, communications for emergency command, rescue operations and supply dispatch have been restored, with full 5G coverage now available in the core disaster area. Power crews are also extending electricity lines deeper into the area, local authorities said. Mud and debris in the core area average about 4 meters deep and reach up to 16 meters in some places, with large rocks covering the surface. A 195-member fire and rescue task force has been divided into three groups rotating through the core zone, focusing on areas including a parking lot and the joint inspection building. Teams are clearing and searching debris layer by layer, using life-detection equipment and search dogs to check newly exposed areas. Since the disaster, fire and rescue forces have made 336 personnel deployments and conducted repeated searches in the core area, said the Ministry of Emergency Management. Heavy machinery is clearing large rocks and deep deposits, allowing firefighters to follow behind and conduct more precise searches around buried buildings, rock piles and sediment-filled river sections. Yang Qiqiao, a firefighter with the Shigatse fire and rescue detachment who was among the first rescuers to reach the disaster area on foot, told CCTV that teams initially relied mainly on manual methods, calling out for survivors, listening for responses and knocking on debris. Search dogs and more detection equipment were added as more equipment reached the core area, he said. Secondary-disaster prevention remains a major focus. The regional authorities said 93 experts and technical personnel are monitoring barrier lakes, the source area of the ice-rock collapse and geological hazards along the road to the border gate. Monitoring continues for possible landslides and mudslides under continued rainfall and higher temperatures. About 150 pieces of professional equipment have been deployed, including 104 sets of slope radar, video monitoring, drones, water-level and meteorological equipment. Rescue sites also have dedicated safety officers, evacuation signals, escape routes and safe assembly areas prepared in advance. Search, monitoring and sanitation teams are working in shifts around the clock, with machinery continuing to operate as personnel rotate. To support road reinforcement and deeper excavation, the Ministry of Emergency Management and the Ministry of Transport have also dispatched 40 sets of temporary roadbed panels, cranes and other equipment from a national highway emergency reserve center in Changji Hui autonomous prefecture, Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region. The panels help prevent excavators, cranes and dump trucks from sinking in mud and soft ground. The equipment has arrived at the rescue site. The ministry said rescue teams will continue adjusting deployments while maintaining intensive searches in the core area. Contact the writers at yangzekun@chinadaily.com.cn Twenty-one people have been confirmed dead, and 541 remain missing after a mudslide struck Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border in Xizang autonomous region on Aug 26, according to the regional government's latest news briefing. The mudslide began with the collapse of a high-altitude glacier in Nepal, which triggered an ice-rock avalanche that developed into a fast-moving debris flow before reaching the port. The disaster has brought renewed attention to the Himalayan valley in which Gyirong sits. Gyirong is one of the main land gateways between China and Nepal. Its geography made it a natural passage between the Qinghai-Xizang Plateau and South Asia. It has been used for more than 1,000 years. Long before the establishment of a modern border crossing, the route carried royal missions, diplomats, religious masters, and traders. In the seventh century, Nepali Princess Bhrikuti traveled through Gyirong on her way to marry Tibetan King Songtsan Gampo. The Buddha statue she was said to have brought was enshrined at Phakpa Lhakhang Temple in modern-day Gyirong county. The same century also saw Tang Dynasty (618-907) envoy Wang Xuance pass through the area on a mission to India in 658. Wang left a cliff inscription as a record of the journey that survives today. In the eighth century, Indian Buddhist master Padmasambhava also traveled through Gyirong, which was described as the first stop on his mission, as he entered Xizang to teach Buddhism. Together, these journeys illustrate Gyirong's long-standing role as a corridor for exchanges between the plateau and South Asia. That role continued into modern times. Gyirong was designated a national first-class land port in 1978 and opened to travelers from third countries in 2017, becoming an important gateway for cross-border travel and trade. The port saw imports and exports worth 4.25 billion yuan ($632.6 million) in 2024, ranking first among ports in the region and accounting for nearly 30 percent of the total China-Nepal trade volume, according to Xinhua News Agency. The mudslide disrupted access through the border area. By Wednesday, road access to the core disaster zone had been largely restored, allowing rescuers and heavy machinery to move in and help with the search for those still missing. Temporary power supply lines to the core disaster area around Gyirong Port in Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region, were fully restored by Thursday evening, ensuring electricity for ongoing search and rescue operations, the China Central Television reported. Power crews had been working around the clock to repair damaged lines since a massive mudslide struck Gyirong Port on Aug 26, cutting off roads, electricity and communications in the hardest-hit area. The restoration of power follows progress in reopening transport and communications links to the disaster zone. National Highway G216, the main land route to Gyirong Port, was fully reopened on Wednesday morning, allowing rescuers, relief supplies and heavy equipment to enter the core area and support deeper searches. Communications have also been restored after crews laid fiber-optic cables, repaired faults, restored base stations and optimized signals. According to local authorities, emergency command, rescue operations and supply dispatch now have uninterrupted communications, while the core disaster area has achieved full 5G coverage. Emergency road reinforcement equipment has been dispatched to Gyirong county in Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region, to support road access and enhance search operations following last week's devastating mudslide, the Ministry of Emergency Management announced on Thursday. Through an emergency coordination mechanism between the Ministry of Emergency Management and the Ministry of Transport, 40 sets of temporary roadbed panels, cranes, and other essential equipment were urgently allocated from a national regional highway emergency equipment reserve center in Changji Hui autonomous prefecture, Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region. Escorted by Xinjiang regional transport authorities, the equipment has now arrived at the rescue site. The temporary roadbed panels are specifically designed for use on mud, soft soil, and other unstable ground, helping to prevent heavy machinery like excavators, cranes, and dump trucks from sinking by distributing their weight. This equipment is urgently required to reinforce damaged roads and support deeper excavation and search operations in the mudslide-affected area, according to the ministry. The massive mudslide, originating on the Nepalese side of the China-Nepal border, struck Gyirong Port on Aug 26, resulting in significant casualties and leaving many people missing. The disaster severely damaged National Highway G216, the main road to the port, complicating access to the core disaster area. Rescue teams have been working to restore and reinforce the land route while expanding search efforts in areas covered by deep mud and debris. A mudslide struck Gyirong Port in Shigatse on Aug 26 after originating on the Nepalese side of China-Nepal border. It caused major casualties and damaged roads, electricity and communications, cutting off access to the core disaster area. After days of continuous efforts, National Highway G216, the main route to the port, reopened on Wednesday. China Daily reporter Palden Nyima is on-site at G216, providing live updates on the latest developments. Tune in to watch the efforts LIVE. A food truck has been deployed in mudslide-affected Gyirong town of Gyirong county recently, providing hot meals to disaster relief volunteers. The truck came from the neighboring Dingri county. After being hit by an earthquake in 2025, Dingri county purchased the truck with funds from East China's Shanghai under an assistance program for Xizang. After Gyirong town was hit by the mudslide, Dingri county soon dispatched the truck to share mobile food services for disaster relief. The death toll from the mudslide at a China-Nepal border port rose to 21 on Wednesday, authorities said, while 541 people remained missing as rescuers expanded deep searches in the disaster's core area after restoring a key land route. Karma Tsetan, chairman of the government of the Xizang autonomous region, gave the figures at a news conference in Gyirong on Wednesday, saying more than 2,300 rescuers had been mobilized for the operation. The mudslide struck Gyirong Port in Shigatse on Aug 26 after originating on the Nepalese side of the border. It caused major casualties and damaged roads, electricity and communications, cutting off access to the core disaster area. The reopening of a section of National Highway G216, the main road leading to the port, has allowed rescuers to move heavy machinery into the hardest-hit areas and intensify searches for people buried beneath thick layers of mud and debris. Karma Tsetan said more than 400 vehicle deployments and more than 8,000 sets of rescue equipment had been mobilized. Drones had made about 800 flights, while 5.43 metric tons of personnel supplies and equipment had been air-dropped into the core area. Before the road was restored, rescuers relied on a combination of land, water and air operations to reach the disaster zone. Some teams approached by boat along waterways, while others trekked for about 12 hours through mountainous terrain. Helicopters made 24 flights to transport rescuers and supplies. Communications have also improved, with 12 base stations restored and lighting and power equipment deployed in the core area, Karma Tsetan said. Rescuers have carried out repeated grid searches covering about 1.59 million square meters since the disaster. More than 10 pieces of heavy machinery have now entered the core area, enabling teams to move from surface searches to more extensive excavation. Ren Wei, executive vice-chairman of the Xizang regional government, said the latest searches are focusing on deeper layers of debris, with mud deposits averaging about 4 meters and reaching as deep as 16 meters in some locations. Large rocks and thick mud have covered the surface, making it difficult to determine what lies underneath, Ren said. Rescue teams have divided the affected area into sections and are using professional detection equipment to search beneath the debris. Priority is being given to locations where people may have been trapped, including a parking lot, a joint inspection building and accommodation buildings. The Ministry of Emergency Management said firefighters have adjusted their strategy as heavy equipment becomes available. Excavators are being used to clear large quantities of debris, while specialized teams conduct detailed searches and use life-detection equipment at targeted locations. Searches are also focusing on buried buildings, riverbanks, gullies and damaged sections of road. Search dogs and life detectors are being used where conditions permit. A forward command post has been established about 1.5 kilometers from Gyirong Port to improve coordination among teams operating close to the disaster area. Yao Xueqin, a member of a Lhasa fire and rescue mobile detachment, said the high-altitude location and extensive damage to roads and communications had made the operation particularly difficult. Thin air, steep slopes and deep mud quickly exhaust rescuers, while damaged roads initially forced teams to rely heavily on walking and drones to move personnel and supplies, Yao said. Disrupted communications also made it difficult for commanders to track teams and issue warnings in real time. Fog, rain and turbulent air currents in the valleys have periodically restricted drone flights and aerial supply operations. The mudslide also drastically changed the terrain and erased familiar landmarks, adding to the difficulties of locating missing people. The reopening of G216 had been a major priority for rescue authorities. Karma Tsetan said crews worked around the clock despite narrow working areas, unstable slopes, rapidly rising water, deep mud and continuing rainfall. A total of 1,333 personnel deployments and 658 equipment deployments were made during the road-reopening operation. By 10 am on Wednesday, the route into the core area had been largely restored, allowing personnel, supplies and heavy machinery to enter by land. China Anneng Group, a national force for disaster engineering rescue and infrastructure construction, said it had deployed 158 rescuers and 33 pieces of equipment on Tuesday night to reinforce water-damaged sections of G216. Crews worked through heavy rain to strengthen temporary roadbeds while monitoring river levels and surrounding slopes. The risk of secondary disasters remains a major concern. More rain is forecast in Gyirong over the next three days, according to the China Meteorological Administration. Three national emergency rescue teams, comprising 39 personnel, have formed a joint monitoring group, the Ministry of Emergency Management said. The teams have accumulated 120 hours of monitoring and collected about 2,700 sets of data on barrier lakes, landslide areas and unstable slopes. Rockfall radar, slope radar and other equipment are monitoring the surrounding mountains, gullies and debris deposits around the clock. Meteorological authorities are providing detailed forecasts every six hours. Yao said rescuers have been instructed to prioritize safety, with teams withdrawing from low-lying valley areas at night and operating in groups with rope protection. Personnel have been told to evacuate immediately if monitoring systems detect signs of danger. Chinese meteorological and water authorities have stepped up cooperation with Nepal following the deadly mudslide that struck the two countries' border, sharing monitoring data and providing weather and hydrological forecasts to support rescue efforts. The Aug 26 disaster originated on the Nepalese side of the border and severely affected Gyirong Port in the Xizang autonomous region. The area's high altitude, complex terrain and rapidly changing weather conditions have made rescue operations particularly challenging. "From late August to early September, plateau shear lines and low vortices are frequently active along the border, with frequent precipitation, posing serious challenges to rescue work," said Ma Xuekuan, chief forecaster at the National Meteorological Center. Following a request from Nepal's Department of Hydrology and Meteorology around noon on Aug 26, the China Meteorological Administration organized an emergency joint consultation with its Nepalese counterpart that afternoon. A second consultation was held on Aug 31, according to Zhang Tianhang, a senior engineer at the World Meteorological Centre Beijing. The two sides also established a WeChat working group for real-time information sharing, allowing them to respond quickly to requests during the emergency. The consultations used MAZU, a Chinese cloud-based early warning system, to jointly assess weather conditions and forecast precipitation in the affected area. China subsequently established a dedicated meteorological support team for Nepal and began providing daily monitoring and forecasting reports in English. "Overall, we have provided seamless forecasting services covering the next 30 days, offering strong support for Nepal's rescue operations," Zhang said. China has also provided Nepal with a customized version of MAZU. Nepal has since requested additional functions, including lightning monitoring, subseasonal to seasonal forecasts and more detailed monitoring and forecasting products. Chinese authorities have shared a range of meteorological products and observational data through the customized version of MAZU, Zhang said. Water authorities have also joined the effort. A barrier lake formed near the confluence of Nepal's Cuojian River and China's Purepu Tsangpo River following the disaster. The Ministry of Water Resources immediately sent a hydrological emergency monitoring team to the area, working with Xizang's regional hydrological and water resources survey authorities. Chinese authorities are providing Nepal with daily updates in five areas, including the development of the barrier lake; potential chain risks from impact pits along the Cuojian River; risks from glacial lakes in the Gyirong Zangbo basin; the development and risk forecasts of newly formed barrier lakes; and emergency hydrological monitoring information. The information is intended to help Nepal assess risks and organize rescue efforts downstream, according to the ministry. Following the disaster, the CMA mobilized resources from the national to local levels. A small ground weather station was installed near the disaster area on the night of Aug 26 and a mobile weather radar was deployed nearby on Sept 1. "These facilities have supplemented our understanding of local weather conditions and improved the precision and accuracy of local forecasts," Ma said. zhaoyimeng@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Tourism in fast lane: Visor down, confidence up
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-05
As night descends over Chongqing, the mind-bending vertical metropolis in Southwest China with layered thoroughfares and surreal architecture turns into a dazzling display of neon. Against this backdrop, a quirky motorcycle-based video trend is taking hold, which many netizens say feels like "visa-on-arrival". The captivating experience involves zipping past illuminated landmarks on a heavy-duty mobile machine, further augmenting the spatial perception of the "eight dimensional" city of mountains and rivers. As the radiant glow of Nanbin Road on the southern bank of the Yangtze River and the towering skyscrapers of the Yuzhong Peninsula evoke scenes from a cyberpunk movie, visitors from around the world are drawn to what has become a new "entry ritual" in Chongqing, the largest municipality in China both in terms of land area and population. For only 198 yuan ($30), enthusiasts can embark on a guided motorcycle video shoot that captures the city's striking night view dotted with landmarks such as the Ciyun Temple, the Hongyadong complex and the Dongshuimen Bridge. These short videos of up to 30 seconds, include iconic gestures and custom soundtracks, offering a unique memento of the city's vibrant nightlife. Tatiana Dvortsova, 35, a marketing specialist from Moscow, Russia, recalled that she first saw the trend on Instagram two months ago. "It made me very curious. Is this for real, I thought," said Dvortsova. Intrigued, she and her husband chose Chongqing as their first stop during their recent 10-day trip to China. On Aug 26, she spent 498 yuan on an upgraded motorcycle tour, opting for several iconic moments such as being swept off her feet by the rider, riding into freedom with her arms open wide, forming a heart with her hands and executing a cool salute while lowering the helmet visor. "I have no words for how excited I was to see the city," Dvortsova said. "The motorcycle experience was scary, but totally worth it." Bai Yu, a former safety instructor and now a thrill rider, advised Dvortsova to clamp her knees to his waist and keep her body tense during the ride. This, he said, would help her maintain balance in case of sudden acceleration or lane switch, ensuring her safety while offering a very exciting experience. Mukhamadeeva Lina Olegovna, 22, a university junior from Moscow, also took the tour. "It was amazing! It was the first such experience of my life," she said. The trend is particularly popular among international visitors, unexpectedly showcasing Chongqing's motorcycle prowess on the global stage. Known as China's "motorcycle capital", the city boasts a unique motorcycle industry and culture. Bai, the rider, noted that around 95 percent of his customers are from foreign countries, including Russia, South Korea, Kazakhstan, Thailand and Singapore. According to Chongqing Daily, by early August, the trend garnered over 1.4 billion views on Chinese video-sharing platform Douyin. On travel platform Trip.com, foreign tourists have described the experience as "like being in a sci-fi movie".

item.title: Serving up emotions: A chat with director Wen Muye
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-04
In an exclusive conversation with Cultural Frontline, director Wen Muye, Egyptian teen star Omar Sherif, and talent producer Mohamed Osama, founder of Dragon Bridge Media, share the story behind the box-office hit Once Upon a Time in the Middle East. For Wen, food is one of life's simplest pleasures — making it a powerful contrast to the abnormal reality of war. From a lavish breakfast to a single fried egg, every dish in the film carries an emotion particular to that moment. The film is also a vivid example of China-Egypt cinematic collaboration. Omar, whose great-grandfather hailed from Shandong province, says his experiences in China have given him a strong sense of belonging and made him feel at home. For Mohamed, cultural exchange is key to creating stories that cross borders. He hopes to help build stronger China-Egypt ties through film and bring more compelling stories to audiences worldwide. item.title: Chinese champion serves up new chapter in Germany
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-04
Chinese champion serves up new chapter in Germany Fan Zhendong to increase profile of sport, exchanges When Fan Zhendong stepped into Dusseldorf's City Hall in August to sign the Golden Book, a historic ledger recording the city's distinguished guests, it felt like more than a ceremonial welcome. Chinese fans had traveled from across Germany — and even from as far away as China — to see him, while Borussia Dusseldorf's table tennis players, coaches, and officials gathered alongside Mayor Stephan Keller to welcome one of the biggest stars of the sport. Two days later, thousands of fans packed Mitsubishi Electric Halle for Fan's first home match in Borussia colors, turning the opening fixture of the Bundesliga season into what club officials described as "a celebration of table tennis". For Fan, the move to the club represents another new beginning in a career already filled with major milestones. For Borussia Dusseldorf, one of Europe's most successful table tennis clubs, it marks the arrival of its first Olympic champion. And for many watching from China and Germany, it signals something bigger — the continuing evolution of a sporting relationship that has connected the two countries for decades. "It's my honor to be here. I'm very excited to start a new adventure," Fan said. "I will try my best to follow Timo's footsteps to build my own legacy for the club and the city." Sporting friendship Few players understand Borussia Dusseldorf better than Timo Boll. The former world No 1 spent 18 years at the club before retiring last summer as one of the greats of European table tennis. His friendship with Fan played a vital part in encouraging the Chinese Olympic champion to choose Dusseldorf as the next stop in his European journey. "The club is very professional, but also like a small family," Boll said. He said Fan needs people he can trust while adjusting to a new environment, and that he will always be available if his friend needs his help. But Boll believes Borussia's close-knit environment will make the transition easy. "The Borussia family will treat him like a son," he said. The friendship between Boll and Fan grew gradually through years of competition at the highest level. "We were opponents, but the clashes between us were always very fair and respectful," Boll said, explaining that this became the foundation for a friendship away from their sporting rivalry. Boll has also come to know a side of Fan that is less visible when the Chinese star is competing in the international spotlight, and describes him as open-minded and curious about life, sports, and culture. Fan follows many sports, enjoys watching live sporting events, and spending time over dinner, Boll said. Despite their age difference, their friendship developed as they spent more time together during tournaments. Head coach Danny Heister believes that the sense of belonging Boll spoke of can help Fan perform at his best. "When Fan feels at home and feels comfortable here, I think he can perform really well," he said. "We'll help him every day with everything we can." For Andreas Preuss, Borussia's long-serving manager, Fan's arrival extends far beyond strengthening the team's lineup. "We never had an Olympic champion in our team, in our club," he said. But Preuss believes the bigger impact may be felt away from the table. "Fan is an inspiration for many things: for business, for marketing, for media interest, for fans, for people, but also for culture exchange between Germany and China," he said. And, after more than four decades working at the club, Preuss said Fan's arrival offers new opportunities to learn. "I learned so much about China in the last weeks and months," he said, adding that he hoped Chinese audiences will similarly learn more about Germany. Preuss also sees Fan's presence as an opportunity for European table tennis to reach a much wider audience, with his popularity drawing more spectators and media attention to the Bundesliga. "Table tennis (in Europe) is like a sleeping lion," Preuss said. "It can grow." The attention surrounding Fan demonstrates the opportunities available to European table tennis, he said, and closer exchanges with China will also offer valuable lessons. "We can learn a lot from China. We can bring many things together, so the potential is very high," he said.

item.title: HK's super connector role highlighted
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-04
HK's super connector role highlighted High-level officials and society leaders gathered in Hong Kong on Thursday for a major conference on integration of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, with keynote speakers highlighting the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region's role as a "super connector" between the Chinese mainland and global markets amid rapidly shifting geopolitical and technological landscapes. The conference, themed "New Dynamics in Asia-Pacific Cooperation, New Opportunities for GBA Connectivity", was co-organized by China Daily and the Hong Kong Coalition, bringing together nearly 300 government officials, consuls general, business leaders and representatives from think tanks, academia and media, as well as public-private sector experts from across Asia. Leung Chun-ying, vice-chairman of the National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, said that collaborative initiatives unveiled recently in data and healthcare between Hong Kong and Nansha in Guangzhou, Guangdong province, underscore the unique role of Hong Kong as a partner and super connector linking the Greater Bay Area with the rest of the world. He said the steps to be taken are clear and necessary — to promote better government-to-business and business-to-business interactions between Hong Kong and Guangdong. "The new momentum generated in recent months through cooperation between Guangdong cities in the Greater Bay Area and Hong Kong will benefit other Asia-Pacific countries and regions," Leung said. Hong Kong SAR Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said in a video speech that the Greater Bay Area is fast becoming one of the most dynamic and integrated economic powerhouses in the world, underscoring Hong Kong's role as the only world city that converges both the China advantage and the global advantage. Lee said that this role takes on new significance this year, as the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Economic Leaders' Meeting will be held in Shenzhen, Guangdong, in November, a historic first for the Greater Bay Area, and Hong Kong will host the APEC Finance Ministers' Meeting in October. He added that the region is ready for the spotlight. Lee said that Hong Kong has a deep and liquid market and a strong pool of financial and professional talent, and the city has become Asia's premier fundraising, asset management and risk management hub. He said the Hong Kong Park of the Hetao Shenzhen-Hong Kong Science and Technology Innovation Cooperation Zone is key to turning cutting-edge ideas into tangible outcomes and world-class research into products, by bringing together Hong Kong's research excellence and the Chinese mainland's advanced manufacturing capabilities. He added that talent is central to Hong Kong's innovation and technology push, while highlighting the "one town, five elements" framework for the Northern Metropolis University Town Area — a hub where universities, research institutes and industries will be set up together to integrate the five elements of education, technology, talent, industry and urban development. "Integrating into and serving overall national development, Hong Kong brings together ideas, capital and talent across boundaries, and connects the Greater Bay Area with global markets. Together, we are not just building the Greater Bay Area. We are shaping a more connected, innovative and prosperous future," Lee said. Qu Yingpu, publisher and editor-in-chief of China Daily, said that the China Daily Hong Kong Edition has chronicled Hong Kong's remarkable voyage — enduring storms, celebrating triumphs and now recording a new era of transformation from stability to prosperity, aligned with the vibrant rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. "Amid shifting communication landscapes and unprecedented global change, we will continue to share the living story of and contribute to this 'one country, two systems', the dynamism of the Greater Bay Area and China's unwavering commitment to an open global economy," he said. Qu also said that he believes that Hong Kong will continue to innovate, leap forward and forge new heights of achievement with its first five-year plan, which is scheduled to be published on Sept 16. Hong Kong SAR Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po stressed connectivity and Hong Kong's role in connecting the world in an age of profound change driven by geopolitics and technological transformation. "As the country's most internationally connected region, the Greater Bay Area presents a strong value proposition for Asia-Pacific collaboration," Chan said. "It rests on a simple conviction: When we partner, we do not merely add up our strengths — we multiply them and extend their reach well beyond Asia." The conference also featured three panel discussions on Hong Kong's financial opportunities in the changing Asia-Pacific landscape, the synergy in commercial aerospace development between the HKSAR and Shenzhen, and education in the artificial intelligence era. Panelists highlighted how Hong Kong can seize opportunities arising from deeper Asia-Pacific economic and trade cooperation to enhance its influence as a global financial hub. Discussions also centered on harnessing the Greater Bay Area's manufacturing capabilities and Hong Kong's strengths, exploring ways to build a collaborative commercial space ecosystem. Panelists also examined how the education sector can reinvent its model with AI to cultivate talent that serves the Greater Bay Area and the Asia-Pacific market.
